title: Mechanism of delayed elastic state absorption versus fatigue failure in cyclic shear of amorphous materials
authors: Samuel B. Walker, Suzanne M. Fielding
abstract: We study cyclic shear in a lattice elastoplastic model of amorphous materials. The model displays a threshold shear amplitude $γ_{\rm c}$, which increases with sample annealing. For imposed amplitudes $γ_0\lesssimγ_{\rm c}$, it shows slow progression to an absorbing elastic state. For $γ_0\gtrsim γ_{\rm c}$, it shows slow fatigue and delayed material failure. Our key contribution is to elucidate a mechanistic understanding of this behaviour. We show that progression to an absorbing state maps to single element diffusion on a finite interval with two absorbing boundaries. We derive expressions for the decay rate of the fraction of active elements, and the survival distribution. The diffusing variable is the local elemental strain, which takes two jumps stroboscopically per cycle. Once the value at any site diffuses below its yielding threshold, the element behaves elastically. This leads to a gradual accumulation of strains just below threshold. For $γ_0\lesssim γ_{\rm c}$ this diffusive behaviour is preceded by many cycles in which cooperativity between elements via stress propagation is also important. For $γ_0 > γ_{\rm c}$, stress propagation dominates and precipitates failure. For $γ_0\gtrsim γ_{\rm c}$, the same accumulation of elements just below local threshold that led to an elastic state for $γ_0\lesssimγ_{\rm c}$ accounts for the fatigue that brings the system to the brink of failure. We evidence this via simulations in which the strain amplitude artificially exceeds $γ_0 $ in each half cycle, before reverting to the system's actual state at $\pmγ_0$ and resuming the next half cycle. During fatigue, the stress-strain slope $dσ/dγ$ evolves towards unity at $|γ|=γ_0^-$, signifying perfect elasticity within cycle, yet towards zero at $|γ|=γ_0^+$, precipitating failure.
summary: This work develops a mechanistic understanding of how amorphous materials fail under cyclic shear, distinguishing between slow elastic absorption and fatigue failure. By modeling the system using a lattice elastoplastic approach and mapping the dynamics to diffusion, the authors show that the same underlying mechanism—the accumulation of elements near the yield threshold—governs both failure modes. This provides a powerful theoretical framework for understanding plasticity in disordered solids.
main_problem: The paper elucidates the mechanistic difference between delayed elastic state absorption and fatigue failure during cyclic shear in amorphous materials.
main_result: The slow accumulation of elements just below the local yielding threshold accounts for both the elastic absorption state (low strain) and the slow fatigue leading to failure (high strain).
method: The study uses a lattice elastoplastic model, mapping the process to single element diffusion on a finite interval with two absorbing boundaries to derive analytical expressions for decay rates.
model_or_system: The system is an amorphous material simulated using a lattice elastoplastic model subjected to cyclic shear. The model incorporates stress propagation via the 2D Eshelby stress propagator.
key_observables: Threshold shear amplitude ($\gamma_c$), plastic activity ($f$), survival function ($S(C)$), and the stress-strain slope ($d\sigma/d\gamma$).
important_parameters: Imposed strain amplitude ($\gamma_0$), sample annealing level ($l_0$), and the cycle number ($C$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the process to single-particle diffusion in the weakly active regime, and assumes the stress propagation can be analyzed via a scalar approach.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate plastic activity decay over cycles, stress-strain curves comparing actual vs. fictitious strain amplitudes, and the spatial distribution of elemental strains showing accumulation near the yielding threshold.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, develops the analytical mapping to diffusion, analyzes the two distinct regimes ($\gamma_0 < \gamma_c$ vs. $\gamma_0 > \gamma_c$), and compares analytical predictions with numerical simulations.
why_interesting: The concepts of non-equilibrium dynamics, threshold phenomena, and the transition between different steady states (absorbing vs. failure) are highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
